intro.title: Know which laws and requirements you must meet
intro.body: This register lists everything the organisation is bound by: laws and regulations, permits and licences, requirements in contracts, industry codes and voluntary commitments. Each **obligation** has an owner, concrete **duties** and a periodic **[[compliance-evaluation|compliance evaluation]]** that checks you still meet it.
steps: Add the obligations that apply to you. Start from the library of common laws, or with the ones that hurt most if missed.
Write the concrete duties and link them to the clauses in your standards.
Plan a yearly evaluation, record the result with documentation and follow up any gaps with a [[nonconformity|deviation]] or a task.

why.body: Every management system standard expects you to know the legal and other requirements that apply, keep that knowledge up to date and evaluate compliance at planned intervals. The register is where an auditor looks first.

empty.title: No obligations registered yet
empty.body: Start with what you already know: the Working Environment Act, the Internal Control Regulations, data protection law, any environmental permit and the key requirements in your largest contracts. The form has a library of common laws to start from.

intro.title: Registering an obligation
intro.body: Describe the obligation and where it comes from. Then list its **duties**: the concrete things an auditor would ask you to show. Tick the standards it concerns so it counts as documentation there.
steps: Pick a law from the library, or fill in the type, owner, authority and a link to the legal text.
Write each duty so it can be checked, and say how the obligation applies to your sites and activities.
Keep the yearly evaluation on, so the owner is reminded to check compliance.

why.body: A register that only names a law is not enough: you need to know which duties apply to you and how. Documented duties, owners and clauses make every evaluation repeatable and show the auditor the obligations were determined systematically.

obligation_type.help: What kind of obligation it is. Laws, regulations and permits are imposed on you; contractual requirements, industry codes and voluntary commitments are accepted by choice but must still be met.
obligation_type.example: A discharge permit is a permit; a customer's supplier code of conduct is a contractual requirement.

status.help: Draft while you are still working out the duties; active once it applies and is evaluated; retired when it no longer applies (the history is kept).
status.example: Mark an obligation as retired when a permit is surrendered or a contract ends.

owner.help: The person who keeps track of the obligation, carries out or arranges the evaluations and is told about changes.
owner.example: The HSE manager owns the Working Environment Act; the data protection officer owns data protection law.

description.help: A short description of what the obligation is about, in plain language.
description.example: Sets limits for noise and dust from the plant and requires quarterly measurements.

issuer.help: The authority or party that imposes the obligation: a legislator, a supervisory authority, a customer or an industry body.
issuer.example: The Labour Inspection Authority, the Data Protection Authority, Customer AS.

reference.help: The official reference, so anyone can find the source: the law or regulation number, the permit number or the contract clause.

valid_until.help: When the obligation stops applying, if it does. For permits, licences and contracts a renewal task is added before this date.
valid_until.example: A discharge permit valid until 31 December 2028.

renewal_lead_days.help: How many days before the end the owner should apply for renewal. Applications often take months, so the default is 90 days.
renewal_lead_days.example: 180 days for a discharge permit that needs a new application to the County Governor.

applicability.help: How the obligation applies to your organisation: which sites, activities, products or people are covered, and anything explicitly out of scope.
applicability.example: Applies to the Drammen plant (painting line and solvent store). The Oslo office is out of scope.

requirements.help: The concrete duties the obligation places on you, one per row. Write them so each can be checked: something you must do, measure, report or keep. Each duty can have its own responsible person and clauses.
requirements.example: Measure noise at the site boundary every quarter; report annual discharges by 1 March.

frameworks.help: The standards the obligation concerns. Ticking one proposes its usual clauses.
frameworks.example: Data protection law concerns GDPR and ISO/IEC 27001.

clause_refs.help: The clauses and articles this obligation documents. They count as documentation on the standards' requirement pages, so an auditor can follow the link both ways.
clause_refs.example: GDPR · 30 for the record of processing; ISO 14001 · 6.1.3 for the register itself.

evaluation.help: A periodic compliance evaluation creates a recurring task for the owner. Each time it is done, the result and documentation are recorded and the next evaluation is planned automatically.
evaluation.example: Evaluate critical permits every quarter and stable laws once a year.

evaluation_lead_days.help: How many days before the due date the evaluation task appears in the owner's My Work.
evaluation_lead_days.example: 14 days gives time to collect measurements before a quarterly evaluation.

intro.title: Keeping an obligation under control
intro.body: The box at the top says what to do next. Below are the **duties** with their documentation and results, the **[[compliance-evaluation|compliance evaluations]]** with evidence and follow-up, and changes coming up. Tasks are in the **Tasks** tab; linked records are under **Related**.
steps: Record an evaluation when it is due: a result per duty, [[audit-finding|findings]] and documentation.
If something is missing, register a [[nonconformity|deviation]] or a follow-up task so it is closed.
Note coming changes and update the duties before they take effect.

why.body: Knowing your obligations is only half the job: you must also check at planned intervals that you meet them, keep evidence of the result and act when you do not. The evaluation history is what demonstrates compliance.

duties.help: Each duty is evaluated on its own and can be documented with records from other modules: a procedure, an inspection, a training record.
duties.example: Duty "Hold safety rounds twice a year", documented by inspection INS-12.

evaluations.help: Each evaluation records whether you met the obligation on that date, per duty and overall. The latest result sets the compliance status and completes the open evaluation task. Anything less than compliant needs findings and a follow-up.
evaluations.example: Quarterly noise measurement within limits: compliant, with the measurement report linked.

evidence.help: Link the records you looked at (documents, inspections, training, measurements), add web links, or choose files uploaded in the Attachments tab.
evidence.example: Measurement report Q3, the sampling log, the authority's receipt for the annual report.

changes.help: Write down changes you hear about before they take effect: amendments, new guidance, rulings or a renegotiated contract. With medium or high impact and a date, a task to prepare is added to My Work.
changes.example: New discharge limits from 1 July next year: high impact, a new filter is needed.

actions.help: Scheduled evaluations, renewal tasks and follow-up tasks are ordinary tasks. They show in the assignee's My Work and are reminded and escalated like any other task.
actions.example: Replace the filter on the painting line by 1 June to meet the new limit.

legal-register.title: Building a register of legal and other requirements

sections.heading: What belongs in the register
sections.body: Anything you are **bound** to meet: laws and regulations, permits and licences, conditions set by an authority, requirements in contracts, industry codes you have signed up to and voluntary commitments you have made publicly. Leave out general good practice that nobody can hold you to.

sections.heading: From a law to concrete requirements
sections.body: A law rarely applies in full. For each obligation, write down **how it applies** (which sites, activities and people) and list the **specific requirements**: what you must do, measure, report or keep. These are what you will check in each evaluation.

sections.heading: Keeping it current
sections.body: Give every obligation an owner who follows changes. Note amendments and new guidance as **change notes**, assess them, and update the requirements when the change takes effect. Retire obligations that no longer apply instead of deleting them, so the history stays.

quiz.question: Which of these belongs in the compliance obligations register?
options: A blog post with tips on energy saving
A customer contract clause requiring ISO 27001 certification
An internal idea for a new product
quiz.explanation: A contractual requirement binds you, so it is a compliance obligation. Tips and ideas do not bind you.

quiz.question: What should you write as the duties of an obligation?
options: The full text of the law
The specific duties that apply to you, each one checkable
quiz.explanation: Concrete, checkable duties make the evaluation repeatable and show how the law applies to you.

sections.heading: Why evaluate at all
sections.body: Standards ask you not only to know your obligations but to **evaluate** at planned intervals whether you meet them. The evaluation is your own check, before an authority or an auditor does it for you.

sections.heading: How often
sections.body: Base the frequency on risk: how serious a breach would be, how often things change and how good your controls are. Quarterly for a critical permit with measured limits, yearly for a stable law with good controls.

sections.heading: Recording the result
sections.body: Record the result, what you looked at and the **evidence**. If you are only partially compliant or non-compliant, register a **deviation** or a **follow-up task** with an owner and a deadline, and evaluate again once it is done.

quiz.question: An evaluation finds that one of three permit conditions is not met. What do you record?
options: Compliant, since most conditions are met
Partially compliant, with a deviation or follow-up task for the unmet condition
quiz.explanation: Record the real result and the gap. The follow-up makes sure it is closed and gives the next evaluation something to check.

quiz.question: What decides how often an obligation is evaluated?
options: The risk of a breach and how often things change
quiz.explanation: A risk-based frequency puts the effort where a breach would hurt most.

sections.heading: Where changes come from
sections.body: New laws and amendments, guidance from authorities, court rulings, new permit conditions and renegotiated contracts. Subscribe to newsletters from the relevant authorities and ask suppliers and customers to tell you about changes.

sections.heading: Note, assess, act
sections.body: Write a **change note** as soon as you hear about a change, with when it takes effect and its likely impact. Assess it: what do you need to change, and by when? Then update the requirements and add actions so you are ready on the day it applies.

quiz.question: An amendment takes effect in six months. When should you note it?
options: As soon as you hear about it
quiz.explanation: Noting it early gives you time to assess the impact and prepare.

list.title: What needs attention
list.body: Obligations that are not fully compliant, not evaluated, without an evaluation plan, overdue or up for renewal. Click a figure to show just those; click again to show all.

list.title: Find the obligations that matter now
list.body: Filter by status and compliance; more filters (type, standard, owner, validity) are under "More filters". Save a combination as a view.

list.title: Register an obligation
list.body: Add a law, permit, contract requirement or commitment, or start from the library of common laws.
